title: To Build a Fire
author: Jack London
sourceEdition: The Century Magazine (1908), Project Gutenberg plain-text edition
sourceJurisdiction: Public domain worldwide (author died 1916; US publication 1908)

premise.en: A man and his dog walk alone through the frozen Yukon, and the man must learn, too late, that the cold does not forgive small mistakes.

summary.en: On a bitterly cold morning, a man sets out across the Yukon trail with only a husky dog for company, ignoring an old-timer's warning that no man should travel alone below fifty degrees. When his boots break through hidden ice, he must build a fire fast to save his wet feet, but the cold and his own small errors work steadily against him.

contentWarning: The story ends with the man freezing to death alone in the snow.

tutorNotes.pronunciation: Watch the long vowel sounds in 'cold,' 'snow,' and 'road,' which learners often shorten. The word 'trail' and 'trial' look similar on the page but sound different, so read them aloud slowly the first few times.
tutorNotes.grammar: This text uses simple and continuous past tenses to describe one action after another, plus a few conditionals like 'if he broke through, he would get wet.' Notice how short, simple relative clauses add detail without stopping the action, as in 'the dog that walked behind him.'
tutorNotes.culture: The story is set in the Yukon during the Klondike Gold Rush, when thousands of people traveled through Canada's far north hoping to find gold, often in weather cold enough to kill an unprepared traveler within hours.
tutorNotes.commonErrors: Learners often confuse 'freeze' (verb, to become solid with cold) and 'frozen' (adjective, already solid with cold); the story uses both. Also watch 'lose' (to no longer have something) versus 'loose' (not tight), since the man both loses feeling in his feet and has loose snow fall on his fire.

gloss.en: a rough path through wild land
a strong dog bred for cold climates
damage to skin caused by extreme cold
a person with long experience of a place
a natural, unlearned way of acting
awkward and lacking skill in movement
a place that protects from weather or danger
to change from frozen to soft or liquid
a calm and serious manner that deserves respect

question.en: Why does the man travel alone, against the old-timer's advice?
What happens to the man's feet, and why is it so dangerous?
Why does the fire under the spruce tree go out?
Why does the man fail when he tries to kill the dog?
What does the story suggest about the difference between the man's instincts and the dog's instincts?

chapters.title: Chapter 1 — The Trail
paragraphs: The morning was cold and gray, and no sun showed in the sky above the frozen Yukon trail.
A man stood at the edge of the trail and looked up, and the sky was clear, though there was no sun.
He read this as a sign of very cold weather, and he was new to the north, on his first winter there.
He did not have much imagination, and he did not think about what fifty degrees below zero truly meant.
He only knew that a man must protect his skin from such cold, and it did not mean anything more to him than that.
Beside him walked a big, gray husky dog, and the dog knew this was no time for traveling.
Its instinct told it a truer story than the man's judgment could.
In fact, it was colder than fifty below, colder than sixty, even seventy, and the dog did not know the numbers, but it knew the danger.
It wanted to lie down in the snow and wait out the storm.
The man, though, had a warm cabin waiting at the end of the trail, and his friends were there already, cooking food by a good fire.
So he pushed on, and the dog followed close behind, and it was unhappy but loyal, its tail curled low against the cold.
The man walked on in silence.
He thought of little beyond the meat and bread he would eat that night, and the dog trotted at his heels, troubled but silent.
At nine o'clock, with no sun yet up, he walked along a frozen creek, and he knew ten more miles would bring him to his friends' camp.
Six hours of fast walking would get him there before dark, and that was true if he did not fall or lose the trail.
He was pleased with his own quick pace in the bitter cold.
As he walked, he watched the ground for a certain kind of danger.
In places, springs flowed under the snow, hiding pools of water beneath thin ice.
Sometimes there was only ice under the snow, and sometimes there was water under the ice as well.
This second kind of trap was very dangerous.
A man might step through it and wet his legs to the knee, and in such cold, getting wet meant real trouble.
He would have to stop and build a fire to dry his clothes, and he had already spotted two traps that morning and stepped around them.
But an hour past midday, on ground that looked perfectly safe, he broke through.
It was not deep, and he pulled himself clear of the water at once, and he was angry at his own carelessness.
Wet feet in such cold could cost a man his toes, or worse, and he climbed the bank and sat down in dry snow.
He knocked the ice from his boot and sock quickly.
His feet were already numb, but he told himself it was nothing serious, and he decided he must build a small fire to dry his boots.
A fire would also warm his aching feet.
He walked toward the trees at the edge of the creek, moving with new urgency.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 — The Fire
paragraphs: He found a group of small spruce trees near the bank, and there he stopped to build his fire.
The trees stood among willow bushes, bare of leaves in winter.
He gathered dry twigs from the brush and laid them on the snow, and he built his pile carefully with cold, clumsy fingers.
He used birch bark from his pocket to catch the first spark, and one match, held steady, gave him a small, hopeful flame.
A fire was absolutely necessary now.
With dry socks and a warm fire, he could face the cold again.
The fire was a success.
In a few minutes he had a roaring blaze, hot against the icy ground, and by this fire he felt safe at last.
He began to knock the ice from his numb feet and hands, and the dog took no comfort from the fire, though.
It lay in the snow a short distance away, watching him closely.
It watched with a strange, careful attention, as if it sensed some danger, and as he worked, he made one great mistake without knowing it yet.
He had built his fire under a large spruce tree, and its branches hung heavy with a whole winter's weight of snow.
Each time he pulled a stick from the brush, he shook the young tree, and the tree trembled slightly, again and again, almost too small to notice.
High above, snow on one branch slipped and fell onto the branch below, and this went on, branch after branch, gathering speed as it fell.
At last a small avalanche struck the man and his fire together.
The fire vanished under a heavy blanket of soft, white snow.
Where it had burned, there was now only a scattered, smoking heap.
The man was shocked, as if he had heard his own death sentence.
For a moment he only stared at the place where the fire had been.
Then the cold bit deep, and he knew he must act fast.
He still had matches, but his stiff fingers could barely hold them.
This time he built his fire out in the open.
He chose a spot far from any tree that might drop its snow.
He gathered dry grass and tiny twigs with fingers that would not obey him.
The numbness had spread from his feet up into his wrists.
He thought of the old-timer who had warned him never to travel alone.
The man had laughed at him then; he was not laughing now.
He struck a match, but it slipped from his numb fingers at once.
He tried again, holding all his matches together in one stiff hand.
At last a small flame began to grow beneath his careful hands.
He fed it the smallest twigs, shielding it from the light wind.
For a moment it seemed the fire might live, and hope returned to him in a sudden, painful rush.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 — The Cold
paragraphs: But his hands were too numb to add the wood with any care.
A piece fell wrong and smothered the tiny flame at once.
The fire went out completely this time.
The man understood, with sudden and terrible clarity, what this truly meant.
The story of a man who freezes to death is always the same.
Now he was living that very story himself.
He panicked, and he began to run along the trail without any plan.
He hoped that movement alone would somehow save him.
The dog ran with him, confused by this sudden burst of speed.
He ran until he could run no longer, then fell into the snow.
He lay there for a while, breathing hard.
He forced himself to stand and try walking once again.
He remembered a story of a man who once survived a terrible storm.
That man had cut open a fresh animal and hidden inside its warm body.
He decided he would kill the dog and warm his hands inside it.
He called to the dog in a strange, urgent voice.
Something in his tone made the animal cautious and afraid.
The dog had never heard the man speak in such a strange way.
It sensed that danger was near and backed slowly away.
It would not come close, no matter how gently he called.
The man crawled toward it on his hands and knees.
But his fingers were too numb now to grip or hold anything.
He could not close his hand around the dog's neck.
After a long struggle, he gave up the attempt entirely.
The dog trotted just out of reach, watching him with wary eyes.
At last the man lay still upon the snow.
He realized then that he was truly going to freeze to death.
Slowly, strangely, the fear began to leave him.
It was not so bad, he told himself, not as bad as he had feared.
There were far worse ways to die, he thought.
A kind of calm settled quietly over his tired mind.
He thought of the men who would find his body the next day.
He imagined walking with them, watching as they found him there.
Then even this last thought drifted slowly away.
Everything grew soft, warm, and pleasantly quiet around him.
He seemed to drift into the most comfortable sleep of his life.
The dog sat facing him for a long time, waiting.
No sign of life ever came again.
Then it turned and trotted away up the trail toward the camp.
It moved swiftly through the twilight, following a trail it knew well.
Behind it, the man sat quietly in the snow.
The cold and the dark settled gently over the silent trail.
